method: Each dialogue was arranged by an AI agent from verified phrases of one scene (no Chinese text was written by the AI), then checked line by line by a second, independent AI agent. Set reviewed: true on a dialogue after a human has checked that it flows naturally.

dialogues.title: Starting dinner and declining seconds
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. The cook calls everyone to the table. 2. As you sit down, you let the elder go first with 'after you'. 3. The host plays down her cooking and invites you to start eating. 4. The usage note says to answer this modesty by praising the food, here said to Auntie with polite 'you'. 5. Pleased by the praise, the host urges you to eat more. 6. 'No thanks, I'm really full' is the keyed reply to exactly this urging.

dialogues.title: Thanks and goodbye after dinner
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. After a meal they cooked for you, you thank both hosts and apologise for the trouble. 2. The usage notes give this 'trouble? nonsense' line as the expected answer. 3. As you get up to leave, you thank them for their hospitality, as guests do at the end of a visit. 4. The host sees you off with 'take care on your way home'. 5. 'Please don't see me out' is the guest's fixed reply to that farewell.

dialogues.title: Arriving at the parents' door
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. The parents open the door with the hosts' usual 'come in, come in'. 2. You greet both parents at once by title, which is the usual greeting at the door. 3. Hosts say this to a guest who has just arrived from a trip. 4. 'It was fine, really' is the guest's set reply to 'you must be tired from the journey'. 5. With the arrival formalities done, the host invites you to sit down.

dialogues.title: Thanking the hosts and saying goodbye
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. At the end of the visit you thank both parents (plural 'you') for their hospitality. 2. A host waves the thanks away, as hosts do when a guest is very polite. 3. You add the guest's apology-cum-thanks to that parent (e.g. the mother who cooked), using polite 'you' for one parent as the usage note prescribes; the plain plural for both is also what the note gives, so this is no register clash. 4. 'Don't treat us like strangers' is the host's answer to a guest who stays this formal, and it often goes with 'don't mention it'. 5. 'Sorry to have bothered you' is how a guest takes leave after imposing on the hosts. 6. 'Take care' is the host's line to a departing guest.

dialogues.title: Arriving with a gift
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. You greet each parent by title when you arrive, before you hand over gifts. 2. The hosts invite you in at the door. 3. Arriving as a couple, you present the little gift 'we' prepared, using polite 'you'. 4. The hosts make the ritual protest that just coming is enough, which is not a real refusal. 5. The usage notes give 'just a small token' as the reply to this protest. 6. 'You're too kind' is the next round of polite protest, as in the modelled exchange. 7. 'Please, do take it' is the warm push to make after a protest. 8. The family accepts the gift with thanks, which ends the ritual.

dialogues.title: Offering a Dutch specialty
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. Once you are in, the host tells you to make yourself at home and sit anywhere. 2. Once seated, you bring out the Dutch specialty and invite them to taste it. 3. The host protests politely that you are too kind. 4. You play the gift down as 'just a little something from me' while holding it out. 5. Hosts may protest two or three times, so a second ritual protest follows. 6. You gently insist once more that they accept the little gift, the reply the usage note gives to this protest. 7. The host finally accepts with thanks.

dialogues.title: Work, money and wedding questions
dialogues.review_note: Lines unchanged; in note 5 'always' became 'commonly' to match the usage note. 1. An elder opens with the standard small-talk question about work. 2. 'Not bad' is a typical modest answer about how things are going. 3. Relatives often move on to income at family gatherings. 4. A vague 'it's OK' is the usual way out of the salary question. 5. The elders switch to the question couples commonly get from relatives: when is the wedding? 6. 'Let's talk about that later', said lightly, gently puts the question off.

dialogues.title: Compliments on your Chinese
dialogues.review_note: Lines unchanged; corrected note 5: the official modesty list gives these two replies as alternatives, not as a pair, but the usage notes do show a deflection followed by a modest remark, so saying both in one turn is natural. 1. The family greets you after your journey. 2. 'It was nothing' is the official reply to 'you must be tired'. 3. Hearing you answer in Chinese, the elder praises your Chinese. 4. 'You flatter me', with polite 'you', is a modest reply that suits an elder. 5. In the same turn you add a modest remark, like the 'you flatter me, I'm still learning' and 'not at all, still a long way to go' pairs in the usage notes, so lines 4 and 5 form one answer.

dialogues.title: New Year call on an aunt
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. On the doorstep, you and your partner say you have come to wish her a Happy New Year. 2. The usage note says to expect 'Happy New Year!' in return. 3. You add the standard health wish for an elder, with polite 'you'. 4. She thanks you and wishes you a happy New Year too, using plain 'you' to a younger guest, as in the official sample this pair comes from.

dialogues.title: Zodiac small talk at New Year
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1. A relative wishes you a Happy New Year. 2. You reply with a wish for the Year of the Goat, which begins at the next Spring Festival (6 Feb 2027). 3. Mentioning the year's animal leads the relative to ask about yours, a question relatives often ask. 4. You answer with your own zodiac animal.

dialogues.title: Telling the waiter what you can't eat
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) The waiter asks whether there is anything you don't eat. 2) You answer that you don't eat pork. 3) The waiter reassures you: a halal restaurant serves no pork. 4) You add your other restriction, a peanut allergy.

dialogues.title: The way to the Bank of China
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You ask a passer-by the way with the basic route question. 2) This is the attested answer to exactly this question. 3) You check whether it is close enough to walk. 4) The passer-by says it is near: five more minutes on foot. 5) You thank them politely for their help.

dialogues.title: Is there a metro station nearby?
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You ask a passer-by whether there is a metro station nearby. 2) They answer with the route, which implies yes: straight on, no turns. 3) You ask how long it takes on foot. 4) They answer with the distance: only 100 metres straight ahead. 5) You thank them politely for their help.

dialogues.title: Thanking staff and leaving a shop
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You thank the assistant as they hand you your purchase. 2) 'You're welcome' is the standard reply to thanks. 3) You say goodbye on your way out. 4) Staff see a leaving customer off with goodbye, take care and come again; their respectful 'you' is the normal staff-to-customer form.

dialogues.title: Parting from your guide until tomorrow
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) At the end of the day you thank your guide or driver with the respectful 'you'. 2) 'You're welcome' is the usual reply to thanks. 3) You will meet again tomorrow, so you say see you tomorrow. 4) A plain goodbye is the attested reply to see you tomorrow.

dialogues.title: Key card, suitcase and finding your room
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) Reception hands over your key card at the end of check-in. 2) As in the source, you then ask where to collect your suitcase. 3) This is the attested answer: staff will bring it up to your room. 4) Hearing about your room, you ask where it is. 5) Staff show the way, as in the attested answer to this question.

dialogues.title: Checking out and leaving your luggage
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You tell reception you are checking out. 2) Reception asks you to wait while they check the room. 3) Meanwhile you ask if you can leave your luggage until your train. 4) The staff member agrees by offering to take your bags.

dialogues.title: Bargaining at a market stall
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) After hearing the price you open the bargaining. 2) This is the seller's attested counter-offer: another 50 yuan off. 3) You accept and take the item. 4) The seller asks which payment app you will use. 5) As in the source dialogue, you answer that you will scan the stall's QR code.

dialogues.title: A cash-only shop
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You ask whether you can pay by credit card. 2) This is the attested answer: the shop only takes cash. 3) You can pay cash, but only with a big note. 4) The cashier takes your 100 and gives you 70 change.

dialogues.title: Ordering mapo tofu, mildly spicy
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You call the waiter. 2) This is the attested reply: sure, which dish would you like? 3) You order a dish, with rice counted in bowls. 4) Mapo tofu is a Sichuan dish, so the waiter asks how spicy you want it. 5) You pick mild as a polite request and explain that you can't eat very spicy food.

dialogues.title: A table for two and a QR-code menu
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) The host welcomes you and asks how many you are. 2) You give the number of people. 3) Once you are seated, staff tell you to scan the table's QR code to order. 4) The QR menu is in Chinese, so you ask for an English menu.

dialogues.title: Buying a train ticket at the counter
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) At the counter you ask for tickets to Beijing on the 14th. 2) This is the clerk's attested answer: the 14th is sold out. 3) As in the source, you ask about the morning of the 15th instead. 4) The clerk implies there are seats and asks which class (the source's 'how many?' line is unverified, so it is rightly left out). 5) You choose second class, the cheaper standard option.

dialogues.title: Taxi to the train station
dialogues.review_note: Changed: line 6 (an 'either' phrase) is now said by the driver instead of by you. A foreign traveller telling a taxi driver where the train station is would sound odd, but a driver who may not stop naturally adds that the station is just round the next corner. 1) Getting in, you address the driver and give your destination. 2) In the same turn, as in the source, you ask how long it will take. 3) This is the driver's attested answer: no traffic, about twenty minutes. 4) On arrival near the station you ask to be dropped here. 5) The driver explains that stopping is not allowed there. 6) In the same turn the driver adds that the station is just after the right turn at the next junction.

dialogues.title: Your ride-hailing driver is at the wrong spot
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) Your ride-hailing driver phones on arrival and asks if you are out yet. 2) You tell the driver exactly where you are standing. 3) The driver apologises and says they will be there right away. 4) When the car pulls up you ask for the boot to be opened for your luggage.

dialogues.title: You spoke too fast
dialogues.review_note: Changed: lines 3 and 4 swapped. 'No problem, if anything's unclear just ask me' did not answer 'you spoke too fast' (a native would slow down or repeat); it is the reply to a request, as in the HSK 3 sample where it answers 'can I look at your notes?', so it now follows your request to write it down. 1) After explaining something, the speaker checks whether you understood. 2) The usage notes give this polite apology as the answer when it was too fast. 3) In the same turn you ask them to write it down. 4) 'No problem' accepts the request, and they add that you can ask about anything unclear.

dialogues.title: How do you read this character?
dialogues.review_note: No change. 1) You warn a host or receptionist that your Chinese is limited. 2) They reassure you and invite you to ask about anything unclear. 3) You take up the offer and point at a character on a sign or menu. 4) Natives do not know every character (the usage notes give 'sorry, I don't know' as a possible answer), so the receptionist looks it up.

dialogues.title: Business card, WeChat and a price list
dialogues.review_note:
No change. (The adding on WeChat happens between lines 2 and 3; the 'who scans whom' line was not inserted because it uses the plain 'you' in a casual register, while you address the client with the polite 'you' throughout.)
1. At a first meeting with a client, you greet them and hand over your business card.
2. The client suggests the everyday alternative of adding each other on WeChat.
3. Once you are connected, you send your price list through the new contact.
4. When you send a file, you add the standard request to check that it arrived.
5. The client confirms receipt with the usual short acknowledgement.
6. You close with the standard offer to get in touch if they need anything.

dialogues.title: Asking a colleague for a number to call back
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. A colleague of your own level (you both use the plain 'you') tells you to call someone back, here Dr Li, as soon as possible.
2. You acknowledge the instruction right away, as work-chat etiquette expects.
3. To act on it, you ask the colleague for Dr Li's mobile number.
4. The colleague asks you to wait a moment while they look it up, as in the official sample where someone is asked to find a phone number.

dialogues.title: First day: welcome and self-introduction
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. The boss opens by welcoming you as a new employee, using the plain 'you' as superiors do.
2. This is the reply the usage notes give to that welcome, thanks plus a commitment, with the polite 'you' to the boss.
3. The boss then asks the newcomer to introduce themselves, as at a first team meeting.
4. You answer with the model self-introduction to a group (swap in your own name, company and role).
5. You end with the usual closing line of a self-introduction to a group.

dialogues.title: Exchanging names with a new business contact
dialogues.review_note:
Changed: line 1 (the polite 'hello', work.introductions.nin-hao) is now said by you instead of by them, so you greet and ask the surname in one turn; in the draft you answered their greeting with a question and never greeted back. All other lines are unchanged.
1. You greet the new business contact politely, as at any first meeting.
2. In the same turn you ask for their surname in the polite way.
3. 'My surname is ...' is the standard answer to that question.
4. Now that you know their name, you add a formal 'pleasure to meet you'.
5. They return the courtesy and ask how they should address you.
6. 'My name is ...' is the answer the dictionary gives to this question.
7. On hearing your name they reply with the very formal first-meeting courtesy 'I've long looked forward to meeting you'.
8. You decline the compliment modestly, the formal reply to praise that the scene's rule recommends.

dialogues.title: Presenting a plan and getting approval
dialogues.review_note:
Changed: 'If anything I've said is wrong, please do correct me' (work.meetings.correct-me) moved from line 3 to line 2. Its usage note and the scene's rule make it the humble closing line of your own presentation, not a reply to praise. The other lines keep their order.
1. You finish presenting your event plan and invite comments.
2. You round off the presentation with the set humble formula asking people to correct you.
3. A colleague gives the positive reply from the same official dialogue.
4. The person in charge closes the discussion by deciding to go ahead with the plan.
5. You thank everyone for their support.
6. The person in charge then ends the meeting.

dialogues.title: Adding a point when time is short
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. Because time is limited, the chair asks everyone to stick to the important points.
2. You keep it short and add just one point.
3. After hearing your point, the chair agrees with it.
4. You say you have one more question.
5. Still short of time, the chair stops the discussion for now, which leaves your question for later.

dialogues.title: Asking a supplier for a better price
dialogues.review_note:
Changed: dropped the last line 'Nothing is final yet. We can discuss it again tomorrow' (work.requests.not-final-yet), a deferral about a pending decision that does not fit a supplier answering a buyer who wants time to think. Added 'I'm afraid that won't work' (work.requests.afraid-not) before the supplier's official reply, so the supplier softly refuses and then offers an alternative, as the scene's rule on declining describes.
1. You praise the supplier's products first, then gently ask for a lower price.
2. The supplier softens the refusal with 'I'm afraid that won't work'.
3. The supplier then offers an alternative, the official reply that a large order makes the price negotiable.
4. You are not ready to commit to a quantity, so you give the non-committal 'let me think it over'.

dialogues.title: Proposing an approach and meeting resistance
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. You propose an approach and ask a colleague of your own level what they think.
2. The colleague says no softly: it is a bit difficult.
3. You acknowledge their view first, then say you see it differently.
4. Rather than refuse outright, the colleague puts off the decision and promises to get back to you.
5. You let them choose the time and ask them to call you back when it suits them.

dialogues.title: Arranging a visit with a client
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. You politely ask a client whether tomorrow would suit them for a visit.
2. The client gives the official reply: you are welcome, and they have nothing planned.
3. Their day is free, so you settle on a time.
4. The client agrees and closes the arrangement.

dialogues.title: A moved meeting that clashes
dialogues.review_note:
No change.
1. You hear that today's meeting has been moved to tomorrow morning.
2. You explain that you already have another meeting tomorrow morning, so the new time does not work.
3. You propose moving the meeting to a different time instead.
4. They agree and close with 'see you then'.
